narrative:
Your application was rejected because the model predicts, with a 99.2% probability, that you will not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. This is an exceptionally high predicted likelihood of failure, meaning the model sees your current academic profile as falling significantly short of what is typically associated with bar exam success. Understanding why this prediction was made — and what could change it — is the purpose of this explanation.

To help make sense of this decision, the model was used to generate "what if" scenarios, known as counterfactuals, that show the minimum changes to your profile that would flip the prediction from "will fail" to "will pass." Think of these as alternative versions of your application that would have led to an approval. Three such scenarios were generated, and they reveal a clear and consistent pattern about what the model considers most critical in your case.

Across all three counterfactual scenarios, only one feature changed: your undergraduate GPA. In every single scenario, a small downward adjustment of 0.1 points in your GPA — from 2.90 to 2.80 — was associated with a predicted pass. While this may seem counterintuitive at first, it reflects how the model weighs your overall profile in combination, and it signals that your undergraduate GPA is the single most pivotal factor the model is responding to in your case. No other features — not your law school grades, your LSAT score, your family income, or your enrollment status — changed in any of the scenarios, meaning the model identified your GPA as the central lever in your predicted outcome.

To put your situation in context, students who passed the bar exam had an average undergraduate GPA of 3.24, compared to your 2.90 — a gap of more than 0.3 points. Similarly, your LSAT score of 34 sits below the average of 37.27 among students who passed, and your law school grades place you in the 2nd decile in both your first and third years, whereas passing students averaged around the 6th decile. These gaps, particularly in law school academic performance, paint a picture of a student whose academic trajectory has consistently trended below what the model associates with bar exam readiness.

The most actionable takeaway here is that while your undergraduate GPA is already set, the broader pattern of your academic performance — especially your law school grades — represents the area where meaningful improvement is most realistic going forward. Strengthening your performance in law school coursework, seeking additional academic support, and investing in structured bar exam preparation would be the most impactful steps you could take to improve your chances of passing and, ultimately, gaining admission.
